title: Tracking state congressional redistricting efforts | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Republicans have come out ahead in the national fight over congressional maps in what could be a major boon to their efforts to protect theirnarrow majorityahead of the midterm elections in November.

But confusion swirls around the future of a map in one state, Missouri, after dueling orders from the US Supreme Court and a federal judge have thrown the state’s map into chaos.

On Tuesday, the US Supreme Court let stand aMissouri Supreme Court decision, blocking a Republican-drawn mapwhich likely would’ve flipped a Democratic seat in that state.

Conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who handles emergency cases rising from parts of the Midwest rejected Missouri’s appeal. Kavanaugh did not explain his reasoning, and there were no dissents.

But minutes later, a federal judge ruling in a separate case ordered the state use the map that favored the GOP. The legal wrangling could land before the Supreme Court again.

CNN is tracking new maps and will continue to update with new state developments.

The court battles come against the backdrop of the Supreme Court’sdecision earlier this year to guta significant part of the Voting Rights Act led to new maps in several Republican states and a decision from Virginia’s highest courtblockeda new Democratic-friendly plan voters had approved.

Those developments marked a major shift in Republicans’ favor in the battle that President Donald Trump and his party launched last year. It had previously appeared headed towards a virtual draw, with Democratic states all but canceling out Republican redraws.

While Republicans might not win every district they’ve targeted on their new maps, the shifts will give them a boost as they try to hold the House in a challenging political environment.

With ahistorically tight House of Representatives, redistricting has become a critical tactic to shaping the midterm races. Redistricting, or the process of redrawing congressional district boundaries, typically takes placejust once a decade, as states respond to updated population counts after thedecennial census.

The redistricting process is different in every state. In some places, state legislators can redraw the map on their own, and all that’s needed is the political will. In other states, the redraw might require changing the constitution, a lengthier process which often involves a direct vote of the people.

Overall, Republicans began the cycle with more opportunities to gain seats through new maps than Democrats did. Republicans have full control of government in more states and many Democratic states haveceded the map-drawing powerto independent commissions, moves some of them have now reversed.

And now that mid-decade redistricting has become another political tool, it shows no signs of slowing down. Maryland voters will consider a measure this November that would give Democrats more freedom to draw a new map and several other states could have new maps before 2028.
